title: Why Is This Giant Pacific Octopus the Worst Mother?
negative_prompt: people, divers, human equipment, aquarium glass, text, letters, numbers, watermark, logo, cartoon, anime, smiling mouth, tears, duplicate mother, more or fewer than eight arms, detached arms, fused anatomy, loose bird eggs, miniature adult hatchlings, graphic death, corpse, rescue, split screen, comic panels, repeated camera, copied background

worlds.base_prompt: Lively cinematic natural-history illustration with anatomically accurate giant Pacific octopus anatomy, crisp phone-size silhouettes, deep teal and turquoise water, coral-orange skin, and pearl-white eggs. Treat every storyboard location and composition as authoritative. Preserve identity through anatomy and palette only; never copy the first frame's camera, rock geometry, pose, or background into a new shot. No text, people, aquarium glass, equipment, gore, human facial expressions, split screens, grids, or panels. Adult female giant Pacific octopus: one anatomically coherent reddish-orange mantle, two clear eyes, eight continuous muscular arms with pale undersides and orderly suction cups. Egg strands: thousands implied through dense curtains of small translucent white teardrop eggs attached to rock, never loose bird-like eggs. Hatchlings: rice-grain scale, translucent orange, eight tiny arms, not miniature adults. Preserve species anatomy and the mother's coral-orange palette through written identity details; do not copy a prior camera, pose, den wall, or background into a new composition.

narration.narration: Why is this giant Pacific octopus the worst mother? She lays tens of thousands of eggs—then stops eating.
Dinner is over. Her eight arms have a nonstop job.
She fans the eggs, then blasts oxygen-rich water across them, again and again, for months.
Months later, dark eyes stare from inside the eggs. She still has not left.
Then—pop. Rice-grain-sized eggs release tiny eight-armed octopuses into open water.
She usually dies soon after. Worst mother? She spent everything so they could hatch.

evidence.claim: The aquarium reports that a female hangs 18,000 to 74,000 eggs from her den roof, lives in the cave for up to six months, fans the eggs or shoots oxygen- and nutrient-rich water over them, does not eat during this time, and usually dies shortly after hatching.
evidence.qualification: Use tens of thousands and months; do not combine these measurements with another octopus species.

evidence.claim: The aquarium reports that a giant Pacific octopus hatches from a rice-grain-sized egg; the tiny hatchling has eight arms with about 14 suckers each and initially drifts in surface waters.
evidence.qualification: Rice-grain-sized describes the egg. Do not depict miniature adult proportions or claim every hatchling survives.
evidence.license: Publicly accessible nonprofit aquarium factual source; summarized, not quoted

prohibited_claims: Do not imply that the mother is choosing death, feels heroic, or understands a future sacrifice.

nature_short.voice_instructions: A fast, playful science storyteller speaking to one friend in natural American English. Keep the delivery near the fastest natural pace this voice can sustain without slurring. Start immediately; make the opening mischievous rather than cruel. Punch WORST MOTHER, DINNER IS OVER, NONSTOP, POP, and EVERYTHING once. Accelerate through the arm-and-siphon mechanism, create a tiny silence before Then—pop, then land the last two questions warmly and decisively. No announcer voice, sleepy documentary cadence, fake grief, dramatic gasp, or extra words. Do not read these directions aloud.
